newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada province paves way for tobacco lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Canada province paves way for tobacco lawsuit.

text.p: Copying a tactic used by U.S. states, British Columbia announced legislation on Monday paving the way for the province to become the first in Canada to sue tobacco companies to recoup medical costs for treating smokers.
The province is believed to be the first government outside the United States to pursue such action against tobacco manufacturers, similar to the approach taken by 37 U.S. states.
Several other Canadian provinces and the Canadian federal government are considering following suit, officials said.

"The legal battle against the tobacco industry is spreading as governments not only in the United States but worldwide believe this is a battle that should be fought and won," said Health Minister Joy MacPhail.
Before British Columbia files its lawsuit, the government said it was first asking the tobacco industry to compensate it voluntarily for tobacco-related illness and smoking prevention programmes.

While the province did not put a figure on that demand, MacPhail estimated the province's direct and indirect medical costs related to smoking and the price of smoking-prevention programmes at about $1.6 billion Canadian ($1.2 billion) a year.

British Columbia Premier Glen Clark rated the chance of tobacco companies agreeing to the proposal as slim and said it was virtually certain the province would go to court in the coming months. He hoped the legal action would prod cigarette makers to negotiate a settlement.

In a letter to the presidents of the three biggest tobacco companies in Canada, MacPhail also demanded they stop marketing aimed at youth and acknowledge publicly that "tobacco is addictive, deadly and causes cancer and lung and heart disease."
Some tobacco companies reacted swiftly and derisively to the province's move.
"It seems as if their announcement is nothing more than a thinly disguised tax grab by another name," said Mary Trudelle, spokeswoman for RJR MacDonald in Toronto.

MacPhail said the province was prepared to consider "other revenue measures such as licensing fees to ensure the industry pays its share of the cost of smoking prevention and the treatment of tobacco-related illnesses."
Anti-smoking activists applauded the news and said it could signal the transformation of the U.S. campaign against tobacco companies into an international effort.
"This is a groundbreaking, landmark announcement," said Rob Cunningham of the Canadian Cancer Society. "It really is a global war."
In the United States, negotiations were set to resume on Monday between state and federal government officials and cigarette makers over a multi-billion dollar settlement.
The incentives for governments to sue in Canada are even greater than in the United States because health care is provided universally and funded publicly.

But the risks are also greater. Damage awards have historically been far lower in Canada than in the United States, and under Canadian law, the government, if it lost, would be forced to pay the industry's legal costs.
Imperial Tobacco Ltd., a unit of Imasco Ltd. is the biggest cigarette company in Canada and is 40 percent owned by B.A.T Industries Plc of Britain.

The second biggest company, Rothmans, Benson and Hedges Inc., is 60 percent owned by Rothmans Inc. and 40 percent by Philip Morris Cos Inc.. Rothmans Inc is a unit of Rothmans International Plc, which is owned by Swiss luxury goods holding company Cie Financiere Richmont AG.
Third-ranked RJR MacDonald is wholly owned by RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. unit R.J. Reynolds Tobacco International. American cigarette brands are also sold in Canada.
